claims.text: The corrosion resistance of high-Cr steels is primarily governed by a Cr-enriched passive oxide layer.
The Cr-enriched passive oxide on these steels consists mainly of Cr2O3.
A dense Cr2O3 passivation film provides corrosion resistance by acting as a physical barrier.
The Cr-rich passive layer actively self-heals after localized damage.
As-processed high-Cr steels possess a native oxide layer composed primarily of Cr2O3.
Aggressive pH, chloride, temperature, and radiation conditions can induce localized damage in the passive film.
The microstructure, thickness, and chemical composition of the Cr-rich passive film mediate corrosion resistance.
The native Cr2O3 layer delays or reduces metal dissolution under aggressive conditions.
Local re-oxidation of chromium replenishes damaged regions of the passive film.
Exceeding the stated environmental boundaries diminishes passive-film integrity and repair capability, increasing corrosion rates.
Samples retaining a uniform, dense Cr-rich oxide layer will have lower corrosion current and higher pitting potential than the mild-condition baseline.
A thinner, more defective oxide film will correlate with increased corrosion rates.
Under mild environmental conditions, the passive film remains largely intact and its self-healing is not challenged.
A pH range of 2 to 7, chloride concentrations up to 0.5 M, temperatures up to 350 °C, and controlled radiation levels represent conditions typical of chemical-processing and nuclear applications.
Outside the stated pH, chloride, temperature, and radiation ranges, mechanisms other than Cr-rich passivation may dominate corrosion behavior.
Cr is the principal passivation-forming element and is strongly associated with pitting resistance.
Oxide-film thickness and continuity can be monitored in situ using XPS or Raman spectroscopy under the proposed test conditions.
High charge-transfer resistance measured by EIS reflects strong passive-barrier integrity.
Comparable corrosion resistance despite a demonstrably compromised Cr-rich layer would falsify the claim that this layer is the primary source of resistance.

contradictions.description: The baseline is tested under mild conditions where the passive film remains intact, yet film-retaining samples under more aggressive conditions are predicted to have significantly lower corrosion than that baseline. The stated mechanism more naturally predicts comparable or worse performance relative to an intact-film mild-condition baseline.

The mechanism predicts that oxide-depleted surfaces can regain protection through rapid Cr re-oxidation, but the falsification rule treats comparable resistance in oxide-depleted samples as falsifying. Comparable resistance after verified film regrowth would instead support the proposed self-healing mechanism; only comparable resistance while the Cr-rich film remains demonstrably compromised is decisive.
